standfirst: The UN's climate secretariat takes the security frame to the European Parliament and calls the summer a continent-wide economic security emergency; the Netherlands' delta commissioner asks the cabinet to double water spending to two per cent of GDP and says plainly that not all damage can now be prevented; and Nepal puts a $4.78 billion reconstruction bill to the world in the same week its scientists agree publicly that they cannot attribute the disaster that caused it.
orientation:
Claims carry one of three marks. **Evidence** is what the sources actually support. **Contested** is where researchers genuinely disagree. **Framing** is advocacy, policy narrative or institutional positioning. **Gap** is a verified absence — something looked for and not found. Sections A and D do not use the marks: A is curriculum reading, D is attributed action.

The week has one shape and it is worth naming before you start. Three institutions in three jurisdictions put a price on climate risk — €180 billion for a European summer, two per cent of Dutch GDP for water, $4.78 billion for a Nepali valley — and in the same seven days the attribution community said out loud that the causal chain behind the week's largest disaster may never be establishable for an event of its kind. Read sections B3 and B5 against each other: the gap between what the science will certify and what the finance is being asked to pay for is the analytically live thing this week, and it is new.

A second thread runs underneath. The security vocabulary is in heavy use everywhere — economic security, energy security, water safety, supply-chain resilience — while the climate referent attaches to it unevenly. Section C is mostly an inventory of which register each jurisdiction reached for.

pushback.target: The standing instruction in `routine/watchlist.md` to watch 'how much security language' Simon Stiell does and does not use — and the temptation to read this week's speech as the climate-security field winning an argument
pushback.text:
The watchlist poses this as a quantity question. It is not, and this week proves it. Stiell used more security language before the European Parliament on 10 September than at any point in his tenure that this digest has recorded. He also used almost none of the field's own register. There is no threat multiplier, no climate-conflict claim, no defence institution, no displacement-as-instability argument. What there is, is inflation, the cost of living, sovereignty, growth, winter fuel, and €180 billion of lost European output. The register is economic security, and the audience was a regulatory committee, not a security one.

So the correct reading is not 'the secretariat has come round'. It is that climate is being argued in whichever register is currently unoccupied. In the United States the security vocabulary survives with the climate referent stripped out of it — the G20 ministerial in Houston this week is titled *Energy Abundance* and runs pillars on energy security and critical minerals (B6). In Europe the climate referent survives by attaching itself to economic security instead. Both are substitutions, and a field that counts only the first as a loss and the second as a win is not measuring anything.

There is a second reason for caution, and it is about evidentiary weight. The €180 billion that carried the speech is not peer-reviewed work: it is *Hot Summer Economics*, a modelling study published by Triodos Bank in August 2026. It may well be right. But the number doing the persuading in the field's most prominent security-framed intervention of the week was produced by a bank, which is a fact worth holding onto at the same time as the argument.

`routine/watchlist.md` has been amended in this commit: the Stiell entry now asks which register he reaches for, not how much security language he uses.

citation.author: Richard H. Ullman
citation.title: Redefining Security
citation.verification_note: Volume, issue, season and pagination confirmed against the Project MUSE record for International Security 8(1), Summer 1983, and the issue index. `routine/curriculum.md` had this right. Read for the second time on this site: the curriculum carried a reset marker dated 2026-09-07 sending the sequence back to its first item, which by the prompt's rule overrides the `next_reading` marker in the 2026-09-06 digest.

foundational.summary: Ullman's argument is a definitional one and it is still the cleanest statement of the move the whole field rests on. He proposes that a threat to national security is anything that, over a relatively brief span of time, sharply degrades the quality of life of a state's inhabitants, or sharply narrows the range of policy choices available to its government and to private actors within it. Two things follow. First, the military-threat definition of security is not neutral: by making states attend to a narrow class of dangers, it causes them to ignore larger ones, and Ullman treats that as a real cost, not a stylistic preference. Second, once degradation of life and narrowing of choice are the criteria, resource scarcity, population pressure and environmental damage qualify on the same terms as invasion — not by analogy, but by the definition itself. Everything after this, including the environmental-security literature and the objections to it, is a fight about whether that definitional move was legitimate.
critiques: The definition is so capacious that almost any adverse trend qualifies. Deudney's 1990 objection, read next week, is that yoking environmental degradation to national security either militarises the environment or empties 'security' of analytical content, and that the second is the likelier outcome.

Ullman offers a criterion but no threshold. 'Sharply' degrades and 'relatively brief' span are doing enormous work and he does not operationalise either, which is why the empirical literature of the 1990s had to build its own thresholds and largely failed to agree on them.

The essay is a product of its moment: the counter-case it argues against is nuclear-era military primacy, and its examples reflect 1983 anxieties about resources and population. A reader coming to it from the 2020s should notice how little of its apparatus is about a physically changing climate, as opposed to scarcity within a stable one.

It assumes the state is the referent object worth securing. The critical strand read in Phase 6 attacks precisely this: whose quality of life, degraded by whom, and who is empowered by the designation.

citation.author: Corinne Lamain
citation.title: 'When the military finds a new territory, it will never leave': 'Vital climate infrastructures' as new climate militarisation strategy? Observations from Nepal
citation.verification_note: Author, title, journal, volume, issue, pagination and DOI verified against the Crossref record (published online 14 October 2025; print issue March 2026). Author affiliation on the record is Erasmus University Rotterdam. The article itself could not be opened — SAGE returned HTTP 403 — so the summary below is built from the publisher's abstract as returned by Crossref, not from the full text. Treat the account of its evidentiary base as thinner than usual.

foundational.summary: Lamain identifies a strand of climate securitisation that the field's own vocabulary tends to miss, because it happens through infrastructure policy rather than through security policy. Her object is what she proposes calling 'vital climate infrastructure': assets whose protection is assigned to military or police actors because they are classified as vital, and which climate mitigation and adaptation investment is steadily expanding. In Nepal she identifies three — hydro-electricity dams, disaster response, and forests — and argues that military and police presence at dams and forests is rising or plausibly about to, with a documented history of harm where it has happened before. Disaster response, she notes, is assigned to the army without it being self-evident that the army is the most effective or appropriate responder. The argument's force is that no securitising speech act is required: the military arrives through an infrastructure classification, and the effect on people's adaptive capacity and disaster preparedness is, on her account, negative. She closes on alternatives that foreground just climate action.
critiques: Chosen deliberately, and the reason is section B. Nepal spent this week running the largest security-force deployment since 2015 as a disaster response, costing a reported $4.78 billion to repair, while its own hydropower infrastructure sat at the centre of the damage. A paper published six months earlier naming hydropower, disaster response and forests as the three sites of climate militarisation in exactly that country is unusually live, and it was written before the event rather than after it.

The abstract's own hedging is visible and should be reported: presence at dams and forests 'is increasing, or could potentially do so'. A claim that is partly about a trend and partly about a possibility is harder to falsify than one that is only about a trend.

The normative conclusion — that this undermines adaptive capacity — does not obviously follow from the descriptive finding. An army may be a poor disaster responder and still be the only organisation in a country with the lift capacity, which is close to the position Nepali officials took in public this week.
Single-country, and the generalisation to 'and beyond' in the abstract is asserted rather than demonstrated. Whether the mechanism travels is exactly what a second case would settle.

developments.title: The UN climate secretariat takes the security frame to the European Parliament, in the economic register
developments.body: Simon Stiell, Executive Secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, told the European Parliament's environment committee in Brussels on 10 September that the climate crisis had become "a continent-wide economic security emergency", citing a European summer of extreme heat that forced mass evacuations, shut down power stations, disrupted trade routes and cut crop yields. He tied the argument to fossil-fuel dependency and a looming winter fuel problem, and told the committee that to be soft on climate action is to be soft on inflation and the cost of living, on sovereignty and security, and on growth. He also said climate impacts are increasingly driving forced migration within and across borders, citing Himalayan floods and heat-driven power outages and water shortages in North Africa. This is the most security-inflected intervention the secretariat has made in the period this digest has covered, and it is worth being precise about which security it invoked.
developments.arc_note: Acceleration of the shift, first visible in the Commission's competitiveness-framed climate work, from arguing climate as a human or military security problem to arguing it as an economic security problem. The novelty here is the actor: the UNFCCC secretariat has structural reasons for caution about security language, and reached for the economic register rather than the field's own.

attribution.note: Attribution studies exist for the underlying European heat: World Weather Attribution published on rapidly worsening European heatwaves on 26 June 2026 and on European drought and water management on 23 July 2026. But the €180 billion figure Stiell used is not an attribution result. It is an economic modelling estimate, and the distinction matters because the speech's persuasive weight sat on the euro number rather than on the attribution science.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Stiell addressed the European Parliament's environment committee in Brussels on 10 September 2026 and described the climate crisis as "a continent-wide economic security emergency". Reported by UN News and carried on the UNFCCC's own news page under the same headline.

source.title: UN climate chief warns political division is undermining fight against 'economic security emergency'

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The €180 billion figure is from *Hot Summer Economics*, published by Triodos Bank in August 2026, which modelled heat-related disruption cutting EU GDP by roughly 1 per cent in 2026 against expected growth of about 1.1 per cent. Its breakdown attributes about 0.6 points to reduced labour productivity, with smaller contributions from crop and dairy yields, constrained nuclear, hydro and thermal generation, and disrupted rail, road and waterway capacity.

source.title: Europe's scorching summer could cost EU economies €180 billion

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Choosing 'economic security emergency' over the field's own vocabulary is a positioning decision, not a description. It buys the urgency of the security register without requiring the secretariat to make any claim about conflict, defence or instability that it would then have to defend — and it was made to a committee whose competence is environmental regulation, not security.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No security institution picked the frame up inside the window. Searched: NATO, the EEAS, and Commission output on defence and resilience between 7 and 13 September. Nothing. The formulation stayed inside the climate-policy system, which is also where UNEP's overshoot frame has so far stayed.

nl_eu.note: Delivered to an EU institution, about EU economies, with a modelled Dutch cost of roughly 0.8 points of growth inside the study it cited.

developments.title: The Dutch delta commissioner asks to double water spending, and says outright that not all the damage can be prevented
developments.body: On Monday 7 September, deltacommissaris Co Verdaas handed the second six-yearly review of the National Deltaprogramma — the *tweede herijking* — to Vincent Karremans, Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management. Its headline conclusion is that continuing on the current course is not an option, and its headline ask is fiscal: spending on water safety, freshwater supply and spatial adaptation should rise from roughly 1 per cent of GDP, about €11 billion a year, to at least 2 per cent. The second half of the message is the one that has not been said this plainly before by the office that holds the Dutch water file. Technical measures remain necessary but are no longer sufficient; society must prepare for disruption and damage that will not be prevented; and the review says in terms that not everything can be done, and not everywhere, and not always.
developments.arc_note: Novel in two respects. The Dutch adaptation requirement has not previously been stated as a share of GDP by the office that holds the mandate, and the acceptance of unpreventable damage is a departure from the register in which Dutch water policy is normally communicated. It cuts against the standing `nl-institution-without-money` trend rather than confirming it: here the institution has named the money.

attribution.note: A policy instrument, not an event. The deltascenarios behind it are projections, not event attribution.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Verdaas, deltacommissaris since 1 December 2023, delivered the tweede herijking to Minister Karremans on 7 September 2026 and called for water spending to rise from about 1 per cent to at least 2 per cent of GDP, against current spending of roughly €11 billion a year. Corroborated by NOS and by TPO, and the delivery is confirmed on the Deltaprogramma's own site.

source.title: Miljarden extra nodig voor wateraanpak, maar zelfs dan niet alle schade te voorkomen

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The review states that technical measures alone cannot prevent all consequences of drought, salinisation and water excess over the long term and with increasing extremes, and that society must be prepared for disruption and damage. A regional water authority's summary of the same document reports its conclusion as 'continuing on the current course is not an option', with spatial adaptation and freshwater security named as the two underfunded priorities.

source.title: Herijking Deltaprogramma benadrukt noodzaak aanvullende maatregelen en keuzes

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: A programme manager working on the IJsselmeer pumping capacity told a regional platform on 7 September that six to seven times the current capacity will ultimately be needed and that the new capacity will already be insufficient by 2045 — a statement that puts a date on the inadequacy of works not yet built.

source.title: Deltacommissaris Co Verdaas: Het leven in de Nederlandse delta gaat ingrijpend veranderen

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Expressing an adaptation requirement as a percentage of GDP, and specifically as a doubling to two per cent, places it on the same rhetorical scale as the NATO defence-spending norm. No source consulted says the echo is deliberate and this digest does not claim it is. It is recorded because the choice of denominator is a communication decision with a known reference point in Dutch political argument, and because it is the form in which the ask will be debated.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No cabinet response inside the window. Prinsjesdag falls on 15 September, two days after the week closes, and the Deltaprogramma 2027 itself is published on that day. The absence of a fiscal answer this week is a calendar artefact, not a refusal.

nl_eu.note: The Dutch item of the week, and the largest single adaptation-finance ask made by a Dutch statutory office in the period this digest covers.

developments.title: The field says in public that it cannot attribute the Himalayan cascade, and may never be able to for events of its kind
developments.body: On 8 September Carbon Brief published a structured Q&A on what can and cannot be said about global warming's role in the 26 August Langtang-Lirung collapse and the Trishuli flood, drawing on seven named scientists across five countries. The collective answer is unusually clean for a live disaster: no formal rapid attribution study has been done; a careful attribution study is needed and has not been carried out; and the deeper problem is that the causality of rock-ice avalanches is messy enough that a definitive single-event attribution may not be achievable at all. What the same scientists say can be stated is that warming makes ice-rock avalanches in the region more likely, and that the mountain in question has warmed measurably. Eighteen days after the event, the field has converged on withholding the specific claim while keeping the general one — and has said so on the record.
developments.arc_note: The novelty is not the absence of a study; it is the collective, on-the-record statement that the absence may be permanent for this hazard class. That marks slope-failure cascades as a category rapid attribution cannot currently serve, at the moment the policy argument most needs it to. It closes out this digest's standing `langtang-attribution` thread on the first question and opens a harder one.

attribution.note: No rapid or formal attribution study exists as of 13 September. Carbon Brief's Q&A quotes Prof Bethan Davies (Newcastle) saying a careful attribution study is needed, and Dr Zeke Hausfather observing that a definitive single-event attribution may prove impossible given the messy causality of rock-ice avalanches and the absence of long observational records of previous collapses. The 2021 Chamoli precedent is cited: that study concluded the individual disaster could not be attributed specifically to climate change.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Carbon Brief's Q&A of 8 September 2026 quotes Dr Umesh Haritashya (Dayton), Dr Kristen Cook (Université Grenoble Alpes), Dr Jakob Steiner (Graz), Prof Bethan Davies (Newcastle), Dr Robert Rohde (Berkeley Earth), Prof Maria Shahgedanova (Reading) and Dr Zeke Hausfather. No formal rapid attribution study has been completed.

source.title: Q&A: What can – and cannot – be said about global warming's role in the 2026 Himalayan floods

claims.label: contested
claims.text: Whether single-event attribution of a rock-ice avalanche is achievable at all is genuinely open among the scientists quoted. Hausfather's position is that a definitive single-event attribution may prove impossible because of the causality involved; Davies's is that a careful attribution study is needed and pending, which presumes it is doable. Steiner takes a third position: the mechanism pre-dates climate change, but the community can be confident the probability has risen. These are not the same claim and the difference is methodological, not rhetorical.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The background trend is documented independently. Silwal and colleagues, publishing in *Global and Planetary Change* in June 2026, find that glacial areas of the Langtang catchment above 4,000 m warmed at 0.31°C per decade over 1960-2023 — more than three times the rate at a lower-elevation station — and that the catchment has lost about 41.5 per cent of its glacier area since the Little Ice Age, with the loss rate rising more than fourfold and accelerating after 2000.

source.title: Glacier changes in Langtang Catchment, Central Nepalese Himalaya from the Little Ice Age (~1815 CE) to 2023 CE

claims.label: framing
claims.text: The restraint is itself doing political work, in both directions. Holding the line protects the credibility of attribution science at the cost of leaving the loudest claim of the week — Nepal's, in B5 — without a certified causal basis. Advocacy communities and their opponents both know this, and the argument has already left the journals: pieces published on both sides in the fortnight after the event treat the attribution gap as the contested ground rather than the physics.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: Searched for a rapid attribution product from World Weather Attribution on the Himalayan event across the 7-13 September window and on WWA's own by-year listing. Nothing. WWA's most recent published study remains 28 August 2026, on Caribbean drought. The asymmetry noted last week holds: the network that can turn a rainfall event around in a fortnight has no product for a slope failure three weeks on.

nl_eu.note: No Dutch or EU link. It matters because it sets the evidentiary ceiling for every climate-attributed loss and damage claim that follows, including those EU member states will be asked to fund.

developments.title: ICIMOD says hazard-specific disaster planning is obsolete, and the monitoring gap gets quantified
developments.body: A SciDev.Net analysis carried on 11 September assembled the physical reconstruction of the 26 August event and drew an institutional conclusion from it. The sequence was a glacier-rock collapse that blocked the Lhende Khola for eighteen to nineteen hours before the natural dam burst — a chain of hazards rather than a single one. Saswata Sanyal of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, whose restraint on attribution this digest recorded last week, is quoted saying that hazard-specific disaster planning is obsolete. Liz Stephens of Reading makes the technical version of the same point: mountain flash floods come from complex hazard chains, not from rainfall. The piece also sets out why detection is hard — only a fraction of Himalayan glaciers are adequately monitored, satellite imagery cannot reliably detect imminent collapses, cloud cover and revisit intervals limit prediction, and the terrain defeats ground sensors.
developments.arc_note: Acceleration of the `highmountain-warning-mismatch` trend opened on 2026-09-06: hazard migrating from the glacial-lake-outburst mode monitoring was built for, to ice-and-rock slope failure it was not. This week the mismatch is stated as a planning doctrine problem by the regional institution rather than inferred by this digest.

attribution.note: Consistent with B3. The article situates the collapse against long-term glacier instability under warming without claiming event attribution.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The 26 August event was a glacier-rock collapse that dammed the Lhende Khola for 18-19 hours before the barrier failed, producing a debris-laden flood — a cascade, not a single hazard. Saswata Sanyal (ICIMOD) is quoted stating that hazard-specific disaster planning is obsolete, and Basanta Raj Adhikari of Tribhuvan University compares the flood's energy to atomic weapons.

source.title: Nepal flood disaster exposes cascading threats in Himalayas

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The detection constraints are specific and physical: only a fraction of Himalayan glaciers receive adequate monitoring; satellite imagery cannot reliably detect imminent collapses; cloud cover and revisit delays limit predictive capability; and remote terrain complicates ground sensor installation. This is the technical floor under every early-warning commitment being made about the region this month.

claims.label: framing
claims.text: 'Obsolete' is an institutional bid as well as a technical judgement. ICIMOD sits on the transboundary data problem at the centre of this hazard class, and a finding that existing planning doctrine has expired is also an argument for a mandate and a budget to replace it. That does not make it wrong; it makes it a move as well as a finding, and it is recorded as both.

claims.label: gap
claims.text: No funded programme follows from it inside the window. Searched for a multi-hazard cascade monitoring commitment, from ICIMOD, the Nepali government, China or any donor, between 7 and 13 September. Nothing dated.

nl_eu.note: No direct link. It matters because 'multi-hazard' is about to become a funding category, and the doctrine being declared obsolete here is the same doctrine European civil-protection instruments are built on.

sources.title: Nepal flood disaster exposes cascading threats in Himalayas

locations.name: ICIMOD, Khumaltar
locations.note: Where the body making the claim sits. Nothing happened here.

developments.dropped: The article relays an attribution of the collapse to glacier instability under long-term warming sourced to Chinese state media. Searched for the underlying Chinese statement and could not find one that makes the attribution claim in those terms. Dropped rather than hedged: an attribution attributed to a state broadcaster, in a week whose whole point is that no attribution exists, is exactly the claim that has to be checked at source.

developments.title: Nepal prices the disaster at $4.78 billion and takes it to the Loss and Damage Fund — with no attribution behind it
developments.body: On Friday 11 September, Lok Bahadur Chhetri, spokesperson for Nepal's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, put the reconstruction bill from the 26 August floods at $4.78 billion: about $57.67 million for short-term recovery over six months and about $4.71 billion for long-term reconstruction. A UN preliminary assessment had put building damage alone at $158 million, noting total losses would be much higher. Three days earlier the Kathmandu Post had reported the financing argument inside the government: Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal saying Nepal prefers grants and aid over loans, with the 2015 earthquake debt as the reference point; Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle acknowledging grants cannot meet the need; and officials describing a claim on the Loss and Damage Fund as potentially symbolic in size but precedent-setting in kind. Prime Minister Balendra Shah is expected to take the case to the UN General Assembly later this month.
developments.arc_note: Novel as a test case rather than as an event. This is the first instance this digest has recorded of a state converting a specific, dated disaster into a Loss and Damage Fund claim in the same fortnight that the attribution community publicly declined to certify the event's causal link. The fund's answer will establish, in practice, what standard of evidence it applies.

attribution.note: See B3. Nepal's climate-justice argument rests on the general proposition that warming makes such events more likely — which the science supports — and not on an event attribution, which does not exist and may not be obtainable.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Nepal's foreign ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri gave reporters a total reconstruction figure of $4.78 billion on 11 September 2026, split $57.67 million short-term and $4.71 billion long-term. A UN preliminary assessment put building damage alone at $158 million.

source.title: Nepal estimates reconstruction after deadly floods to cost nearly $7 billion
source.publisher: ABC News (Australia), citing Reuters and AP

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: The grants-versus-loans argument is on the record and unresolved. Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal: though not officially decided, Nepal prefers grants and aid over loans. Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle concedes grants cannot meet all needs. A former National Planning Commission vice-chairman, Govinda Raj Pokharel, argues it is impossible to secure enough grants from conventional development partners alone and recommends soft loans. A post-disaster needs assessment was expected within five weeks of 8 September.

source.title: Nepal looks for grants for flood recovery, but loans may be unavoidable

claims.label: framing
claims.text: Nepal's officials frame the ask as shared responsibility: a country that contributes little to climate change is facing a disaster of this scale, so why should the cost not be shared. This is the loss and damage argument in its cleanest political form and it is being made without the causal certificate the fund's sceptics will ask for. Nepali officials themselves describe the likely sum as symbolic, which indicates that the point of the claim is the precedent rather than the money.

claims.label: evidence
claims.text: Nepal had already narrowed the claim before this week. On 3 September, Foreign Minister Khanal clarified that Nepal had not demanded climate damage compensation from India, China or the United States, and would instead seek support through the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement machinery. The bilateral route was closed and the multilateral one kept open — which is what makes the Loss and Damage Fund the whole of the strategy rather than one option in it.

source.title: The diplomatic implications of Nepal's retreat from 'climate compensation'

developments.title: The US moves to erase power-plant carbon limits, timed to a G20 ministerial on 'energy abundance'
developments.body: On 13 September, Bloomberg reported that the Environmental Protection Agency was poised to rescind carbon standards for coal- and gas-fired power plants as soon as Monday, with a separate proposal to repeal the finding that greenhouse gases from power plants pose a threat. The timing is the part that belongs in this digest: the announcement was expected on the sidelines of the G20 energy ministerial in Houston, held 14-16 September under the US presidency and titled the *Energy Abundance* ministerial, whose three pillars are energy security and affordable baseload, permitting and regulatory efficiency, and critical minerals and resilient supply chains. Note what survives and what does not. The security vocabulary is fully intact — energy security, resilient supply chains, critical minerals. The climate referent has been removed from it.
developments.arc_note: Continues the `us-vehicle-removal` trend: the removal of climate from security instruments rather than merely from security language. This week's instance is the inverse and is worth stating separately — the security language is being retained with the climate object cut out, which is a different operation from deleting the language.

developments.title: UNGA81 opens with climate among six priorities, and nowhere near the security register
developments.body: Khalilur Rahman of Bangladesh gavelled open the 81st session of the General Assembly on 8 September under the theme 'Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all', with six stated priorities of which one is to step up climate action. His opening statement is worth reading for where climate sits in it. Climate appears under adaptation and resilience, under ocean and biodiversity health, and under the existential exposure of small island developing states and low-lying coastal nations. Refugees, migrants and displaced communities appear under humanitarian space and rights, not under instability. Peace and security appear separately, framed around prevention and political solutions. A president from the country that is the field's most cited example of climate vulnerability opened the session without joining the two files.
developments.arc_note: A repeat of the pattern this digest has recorded since week one: climate is handled in the development and adaptation register at the UN's political centre, while the security register is reserved for conflict. The Security Council's September programme of work, under the French presidency, confirms it by omission.

moves.title: The UNFCCC secretariat borrows economic security rather than climate security
moves.actor: UN Framework Convention on Climate Change secretariat; Executive Secretary Simon Stiell
moves.body: Stiell — UNFCCC Executive Secretary, a role re-confirmed this week against UNFCCC and UN News coverage of the appearance itself; the term dates in `routine/watchlist.md` are from August 2022 and a June 2025 reappointment, verified in August 2026 and not re-checked this week — appeared before the European Parliament's ENVI committee and made the most security-inflected argument of his tenure, in an economic register. He told members that climate has become a continent-wide economic security emergency, that treating it as partisan territory in culture wars is palpably false, and that being soft on climate action means being soft on inflation, cost of living, sovereignty, security and growth. He carried a €180 billion figure for the summer's European losses and a warning about the coming winter's fuel costs, and he named forced migration, Himalayan floods and North African outages in the same breath. He did not use the word overshoot, and he made no claim about conflict.
moves.stated_rationale: That Europe's economic exposure to climate impacts is now large enough to be a first-order political fact, that the costs are traceable to fossil-fuel dependency, and that the clean energy transition is the route out. His supporting energy figures — a share of European power now met by renewables, and savings on avoided gas imports — appear only in search-returned coverage and are not repeated here.
moves.inference: The secretariat's traditional audience is a party to the convention. Its largest historical interlocutor withdrew from the convention and from the IPCC on 7 January 2026. Arguing in Brussels, in economic terms, to a regulatory committee, is what is left: the security urgency is borrowed because the convention's own leverage has thinned, and the economic register is borrowed because the military-security register in the transatlantic space is currently occupied by an energy agenda with no climate referent. moves.title: The Dutch delta commissioner puts adaptation on a percent-of-GDP footing, and concedes unpreventable damage
moves.actor: Deltacommissaris Co Verdaas, in office since 1 December 2023; delivered to Vincent Karremans, Minister of Infrastructure and Water Management
moves.body: Verdaas handed the second six-yearly review of the National Deltaprogramma to Karremans on 7 September, eight days before Prinsjesdag and the publication of the Deltaprogramma 2027 that the review underpins. Two things were done at once. Financially, the ask was stated as a share of national output for the first time in this office's public argument: from about 1 per cent of GDP to at least 2 per cent, doubling roughly €11 billion a year. Politically, the review conceded that technical measures cannot prevent all consequences of drought, salinisation and water excess, that society must prepare for disruption and damage, and that not everything can be done everywhere and always. Preparation for a new generation of Deltaworks — replacement of the Maeslantkering, decisions on the Rhine-Maas estuary, new pumping capacity at IJmuiden and possibly the Afsluitdijk — is said to have to start now.
moves.stated_rationale: That climate change, salinisation and rising water demand are outpacing the programme's planning assumptions, that continuing on the current course is not an option, and that spatial adaptation and freshwater security are the two underfunded priorities.
moves.inference: Conceding unpreventable damage is the expensive half of this move and it is what makes the fiscal ask credible rather than routine. A water authority that says it can hold the line has to be funded to hold the line; one that says the line will be crossed in places is asking to be funded for something harder to audit. Choosing a percent-of-GDP denominator eight days before the budget puts the number into the frame in which Dutch spending arguments are currently conducted. Whether that was the intent is not established by any source read here.

moves.title: Nepal converts a disaster into a multilateral claim, having already closed the bilateral route
moves.actor: Government of Nepal: Prime Minister Balendra Shah; Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal; Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle; foreign ministry spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri
moves.body: Across five days Nepal assembled a position. On 8 September the financing debate went public: grants preferred, loans probably unavoidable, a post-disaster needs assessment expected within five weeks, and the Loss and Damage Fund named as a route whose value officials themselves described as potentially symbolic but precedent-setting. On 11 September the foreign ministry put the reconstruction bill at $4.78 billion. Shah is expected to take the case to the General Assembly during high-level week. The move was set up the week before, when Khanal clarified on 3 September that Nepal was not demanding compensation from India, China or the United States and would work through the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement instead — closing the bilateral door before opening the multilateral one.
moves.stated_rationale: That a country contributing little to climate change should not bear alone the cost of a disaster of this scale, and that the multilateral machinery rather than individual emitters is the appropriate venue.
moves.inference: Two readings, and they are not exclusive. Sequencing the bilateral disavowal before the multilateral claim protects the relationships with the two neighbours Nepal cannot afford to antagonise, one of which holds the hydrological data it wants. And describing the expected sum as symbolic while pursuing it anyway indicates the target is the precedent — a fund disbursement for an event with no attribution study would set a standard of evidence that every subsequent claimant could use. That would be a considerable prize for a small state to win from a bad month, and it is the only reading under which the effort makes sense against the size of the likely cheque.

moves.title: NATO's annual climate security assessment has now missed two cycles, without a word
moves.actor: NATO; the office of the Secretary-General
moves.body: This is the week's quiet move and it is an absence. NATO's Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment is described on NATO's own topic page as the Secretary-General's annual assessment, and it ran annually from 2021: action plan 14 June 2021, assessments 28 June 2022, 11 July 2023, 9 July 2024. Re-checked this week against the topic page: there is no 2025 edition and no 2026 edition, and the page's most recent news item is the July 2024 Washington summit. Two annual cycles have now passed. The nearest substitute is the Science and Technology Organization's SAS-182 final report *The Effects of Climate Change on Security*, published January 2026 — a research task group output that recommends the Climate Change and Security Action Plan be modified to turn knowledge into action. It is not a Secretary-General's assessment and does not replace one. The IMCCS pattern runs parallel: no World Climate and Security Report since the 2024 edition, and the most recent item on the council's own site is an open letter of 23 October 2025.
moves.stated_rationale: None has been given. No NATO statement announcing discontinuation, suspension, replacement or delay could be found. That is the substance of the finding: an annual instrument stopped without an announcement, which is the form institutional de-prioritisation usually takes.
moves.inference: One cycle missed is a scheduling problem; two is a decision, taken somewhere, by someone. The most economical reading is that the assessment's continuation was contingent on a political consensus that no longer holds among allies, and that the STO route — a technical report from a research task group, which requires no Secretary-General's signature — is where the analytical work has been allowed to continue. This is inference and the confidence below reflects it: nothing found this week establishes that any decision was taken at all, and an instrument can lapse through neglect as easily as through choice.

The watchlist's underlying argument — that Dutch climate-security research demand which actually pays has been domestic-order demand rather than defence demand — needs qualifying rather than deleting: a defence strategy now exists, HCSS has engaged it, and whether the engagement is commissioned or unsolicited is the open question. `routine/watchlist.md` has been amended.

**The Center for Climate and Security is not silent, and last week's reading of its venue needs correcting.** climateandsecurity.org's blog shows nothing since April 2026, which in isolation reads as a shutdown. It is a move: CCS output now appears on the parent Council on Strategic Risks site, which published two CCS-branded items across 1 and 10 September. The `csr-ccs-staffing` thread stays open on funding and staffing, but the activity question is answered.

**adelphi:** nothing in the window; the Berlin Climate and Security Conference remains scheduled for 6 October.

**SIPRI:** no climate-security publication datable to 7-13 September found.

**World Weather Attribution:** nothing published in the window; its most recent study remains 28 August 2026 on Caribbean drought. Added to the roster last week precisely because attribution institutions now set the terms of argument faster than security institutions respond, WWA's first recorded week of silence coincides with the week the attribution question became the central political fact of the Nepal file. That is not a criticism of WWA — B3 explains why the hazard class may be beyond rapid methods — but it is the sharpest available illustration of the limit.

**UN Climate Security Mechanism:** no output in the window. **ICIMOD** was the week's most active roster member (B4) and the **Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat** produced nothing after last week's Belau declaration. **No move from the Gulf states or the African Union.** AOSIS produced no statement in the window, but its chair is now identified for the first time (see Multilateral).

watch.title: Prinsjesdag: what the cabinet does with a two-per-cent ask
watch.note: 15 September, two days after this week closes, and three things resolve on the day. Whether the Deltaprogramma 2027 and the accompanying budget documents acknowledge any part of Verdaas's 1-to-2-per-cent-of-GDP ask, or restate the Deltafonds as planned. Whether the €5 million structural line for the *Defensiestrategie voor Klimaatverandering en Veiligheid – Klimaatparaat* survives into the 2027 Defensiebegroting and whether it grows. watch.title: Whether the Loss and Damage Fund answers an unattributed event
watch.note: The general debate opens 22 September and the high-level meeting on climate action and just transition falls on 23 September. Two datable questions. Whether Balendra Shah puts the $4.78 billion figure and a Loss and Damage Fund claim on the General Assembly floor, and whether the fund's board convenes the extraordinary meeting its members were reported to be seeking on 2 September. The second is the real test: a disbursement for an event with no attribution study, or a refusal on those grounds, sets the evidentiary standard by practice for every claim after it. Watch also whether 'overshoot' appears in the Climate Summit's framing — the tell for D1 of the 2026-09-06 digest, which has not yet fired.

watch.title: Whether the EPA rescission lands at Houston, and what the ministerial communiqué says
watch.note: The rescission was expected on 14 September and the G20 energy ministerial ran 14-16 September. Three checkable outcomes: whether the rescission was in fact announced and on what date; whether the separate proposal against the power-plant endangerment finding followed; and whether any ministerial outcome document mentions climate at all, given three pillars that name energy security, permitting and critical minerals and do not name it. A communiqué that discusses supply-chain resilience without a climate referent would confirm the substitution this digest describes in B6 rather than leaving it as a reading of branding.

active_trends.text: US removal of climate from security *vehicles*, not just language. This week adds the inverse operation and it may be the more durable one: the security vocabulary retained with the climate referent removed, as at the G20 'Energy Abundance' ministerial.
US adaptation surviving only where reframed as disaster operations.
UNSC shift from "climate security" to "natural resource governance". September's programme of work under the French presidency contains neither.

Retreat from binding multilateral environmental instruments (UNCCD drought, twice). Per the 2026-09-06 pushback, do not extend this trend to cover institutional candour about overshoot; the two are different acts and merging them makes the trend unfalsifiable.

Dutch institutional creation with fiscal non-commitment. Note a counter-instance this week: the deltacommissaris named the money before the budget rather than after it. The defence side still fits the trend — a strategy with €5m structural and no action plan two months on.
Dutch public-opinion decline against the international average. Carried forward but not re-verified for three consecutive weeks; treat as stale until refreshed.

Overshoot moving from a risk to a planning premise. No security institution adopted the term this week, and the UNFCCC's own executive secretary did not use it in his most security-framed speech to date. The tell has not fired.

High-mountain hazard migrating from the glacial-lake-outburst mode that monitoring was built for to ice-and-rock slope failure that it was not, across borders where no data-sharing mechanism exists. ICIMOD now states the planning-doctrine half of this directly: hazard-specific disaster planning is obsolete.

The widening gap between what event attribution will certify and what climate finance is being asked to pay for. Rock-ice avalanches may be permanently outside single-event attribution while being exactly the hazard class generating the largest new loss-and-damage claims. Watch which gives first: the methods, the standard of evidence, or the claim.

Climate argued in whichever security register is locally unoccupied — economic security in Europe, energy security in the US — rather than in the field's own. Counting the first as a win and the second as a loss measures nothing; the question is which referent the security vocabulary is attached to.

Added: the PSI site and Clingendael describe van Schaik's role differently, which is worth resolving alongside this.

The series ran 2022, 2023, 2024 and has now missed two annual cycles, with no announcement of discontinuation, suspension or replacement. Promoted to a move this week (D5). The thread stays open because what is missing is not the document but any NATO statement about it.

Re-checked against imccs.org: no report since the 2024 edition, and the most recent item of any kind on the site is an open letter of 23 October 2025 on clean energy investment in NATO spending targets. Same shape as the NATO thread and probably the same cause.

CSM funding trajectory. Not advanced this week; no CSM output in the window and the annual financial report was not retrieved. Structure is documented through 2028, volumes are not, and the volumes are the part that would show a trajectory.

MFF 2028-2034 climate/security line. The catalogue entry exists; the page returned empty content and could not be read. Retrieve it next week — it is the most likely single source for whether any security-tagged climate earmark exists.

Chinese 2026 defence doctrine on climate — gap. Re-checked; unchanged. The Chinese observable remains negative and specific: no transboundary hydrological data agreement on the Nepal border, on a file where China already shares data year-round with five Mekong states. Capability is not the constraint.

Any Indian security document on climate — gap. Re-checked; unchanged. India's one dated ministerial engagement on energy and security this week was with the US-hosted G20 'Energy Abundance' ministerial, which has no climate pillar.
Swiss Re sigma citation for the $424bn 2025 protection gap. Resolved this week now that the retrieval constraint has lifted enough to pursue it.
open_threads.resolution: The citation is **sigma 1/2026**, *Natural catastrophes in 2025: the persistent rise of wildfire and storm risk*, Swiss Re Institute. The protection gap of $424 billion for 2025, up from $395 billion in 2024, with the natural catastrophe resilience index broadly stable at 27.3 per cent, comes from the Institute's Natural Catastrophe Insurance Resilience Index and is expressed in premium-equivalent terms. Caveat on strength: swissre.com returned HTTP 403 and the mirrored PDF's text could not be extracted, so the sigma number and figures are corroborated across Swiss Re's own social post and several independent trade reports rather than read off the document. The number may now be cited with the sigma reference.

open_threads.text: Whether any event attribution study of the 26 August Langtang-Lirung cascade appears. Substantially advanced this week and the answer is harder than the question assumed. Carbon Brief's Q&A of 8 September, drawing on seven named scientists, records that no rapid or formal study exists and that a definitive single-event attribution of a rock-ice avalanche may not be achievable at all, citing the 2021 Chamoli precedent. The ice-and-rock-avalanche account has prevailed over the earlier glacial-lake-drainage account. Still open on whether anyone attempts a study; newly open on whether the hazard class is permanently outside rapid attribution's reach, which is the more consequential question.
What the HiRISK consortium is: membership, funding, institutional home.
open_threads.resolution: Resolved from hirisk.org, which was opened and read this week. HiRISK describes itself as 'a loose consortium of experts from High Mountain Asia and beyond', producing open risk datasets, dashboards, an expert database, risk assessments and peer-reviewed papers. Its member organisations are listed by country and include the Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee, the University of Central Asia in Tajikistan, a research group in Pakistan, a mountain-hazards institute in China, a hydrological institute in Bhutan, and two regional agencies — the Aga Khan Agency for Habitat among them. Its stated support comes from Geo Mountains and from the Glacier and Permafrost Hazards in Mountains standing group of the International Association of Cryospheric Sciences and the International Permafrost Association. Funding amounts and sources are not disclosed, no individuals are named on the site, and the site is labelled a beta version. Verdict for citation purposes: a real, regionally-rooted, multi-institution network — and one that includes a Chinese institute, which matters on a file whose central problem is a closed border — but informal, unfunded so far as the public record shows, and not an authority in the sense a named institution would be. Cite it as a consortium finding, attribute it to the consortium, and do not upgrade it to institutional authority. Two member labels on the site could not be expanded against any independent source and are therefore described generically above rather than spelled out.

open_threads.text: What standard of evidence the Loss and Damage Fund applies to a claim arising from an event that has no attribution study and may never get one. Nepal's $4.78 billion reconstruction bill and its stated intention to approach the fund make this the first live test. The answer will be established by practice — a disbursement, a refusal, or a silence — before any methodology for attributing rock-ice avalanches exists. Watch the board's handling of the extraordinary meeting its members were reported to be seeking on 2 September.

Whether any part of the deltacommissaris's ask — 1 per cent of GDP to at least 2, roughly €11 billion a year to roughly €22 billion — survives into a government commitment, and whether the review's concession that some damage will not be prevented is adopted in cabinet language or quietly dropped from it. Prinsjesdag on 15 September is the first datable checkpoint; the cabinet's formal reaction to the Deltaprogramma 2027 is the second.

UNSG succession, finalisation Aug-Oct 2026. Straw polls held 30 July and 21 August, Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett leading the second on eight 'encourage' votes, with Rebeca Grynspan and Rafael Grossi on seven each. Further rounds expected in September under the French presidency but not during high-level week; colour-coded ballots expected later in the process. Guterres's term ends 31 December 2026. Nothing found on what any candidate has said about Council competence over climate — that remains the highest-value unanswered question here.

Whether 'overshoot' is adopted as a planning premise by security institutions or stays inside the climate-policy system. Negative evidence this week and it is informative: the UNFCCC's executive secretary made his most security-framed intervention to date and did not use the term. The tell has not fired.

Whether AOSIS's legal-character defence of 1.5°C holds through UNGA81 and COP31. Substance unchanged; no AOSIS statement in the window. The bloc now has a nameable principal for the first time in this digest: H.E. Ms Ilana Victorya Seid, Permanent Representative of Palau to the UN since 2021, AOSIS chair for 2025-2026.

Whether the pre-event-indications finding produces a funded glacier-hazard early-warning programme, and whether it can survive the China-Nepal data-sharing wall. Provenance now established (see the resolved `hirisk-consortium-identity` thread): a real multi-institution network, informal and with no disclosed funding. Outcome still open, and no funded programme appeared this week.

Whether Nepal's restriction of foreign search-and-rescue becomes a precedent or an episode. The file has turned: Nepal's active demand is now inward — a real-time data-sharing agreement with China at ten-minute intervals, on the model of its arrangement with India — rather than a restriction on inbound assistance. Still open on whether any transboundary early-warning mechanism emerges.

Whether the UNFCCC secretariat's economic-security framing is picked up by anyone outside the climate-policy system, and in particular whether any EU security institution — the EEAS, a Commission DG on the defence side, or a member-state ministry — adopts the formulation. If it stays inside ENVI and the climate press, it was a rhetorical escalation; if a security institution repeats it, the register shift is real.

Whether the deltacommissaris's two-per-cent-of-GDP ask converts into any government commitment, and whether the concession that some damage cannot be prevented survives into cabinet language. First checkpoint Prinsjesdag, 15 September.

Whether Nepal's $4.78 billion bill produces a Loss and Damage Fund response, and on what evidentiary basis given that no attribution study exists. Also whether the grants-versus-loans argument resolves towards debt, which would make the climate-justice framing politically necessary rather than optional.

Whether the rescission was announced as expected on 14 September, whether the separate proposal against the power-plant endangerment finding follows, and whether the Houston ministerial's outcome document mentions climate at all.

Whether NATO ever states what happened to the Secretary-General's annual Climate Change and Security Impact Assessment, now two cycles missed without announcement, and whether the STO's SAS-182 route becomes the permanent home of the analytical work. A statement either way would close this; continued silence is itself the finding and should be re-recorded each week rather than assumed.
